story.title: A Promise Kept
paragraphs_en: The telephone kept on the table beside the bed rang sharply. The black polished telephone contrasted the brilliantly lit white room. The nurse came in from the other room and answered. “Hullo? Renata?” “May I know who I am speaking to please?” “May I speak to Renata Berger please? I am her husband, Herz Berger. Tell her my name, she would recognize.” The burgundy colored train with the yellow characters ‘PENNSYLVANIA’ stopped on the station of Philadelphia. Herz Berger stepped out of the passenger coach of second class. He had a long black overcoat draped over his hunched back. There was a silhouette of a six-point star etched on his coat. At one time, there was The Star of David sown there. It was just the shadow left now. A long white beard overlapped the overcoat. Mr. Berger walked slowly, measuring every step judiciously. Renata?” “May I know who I am speaking to please?” “May I speak to Renata Berger please? I am her husband, Herz Berger. Tell her my name, she would recognize.” The burgundy colored train with the yellow characters ‘PENNSYLVANIA’ stopped on the station of Philadelphia. Herz Berger stepped out of the passenger coach of second class. He had a long black overcoat draped over his hunched back. There was a silhouette of a six-point star etched on his coat. At one time, there was The Star of David sown there. It was just the shadow left now. A long white beard overlapped the overcoat. Mr Berger walked slowly, measuring every step judiciously.

Herz was brought into the small room by the nurse. Renata sat on the bed, facing on the other side, staring at the wall. She was in a long black frock with grey hair tied in an untidy bun. “Renata?” He whispered from underneath the unkempt mustache. “Mr. Berger, I told you that Mrs. Berger is suffering from Retrograde amnesia. She does not even remember her name. That is exactly why she has been kept in this nursing home.” Herz tilted his head towards the nurse, still looking at the ground. Tears welled up in his wrinkled eyes. It took him great courage to ask, “Is there any chance she can get better?”

“Renata, I promise I will see you very soon,” I said at the Port of Amsterdam as she prepared to leave with some fellow Jews. I knew sending her to the New World was not safe, especially with German U- boats scanning the Atlantic. But I had no other alternative to ensure she survives. She would wait for me there. She would live in the Emergency Refugee Shelter in New York. As soon as the war is over, I would travel there too. I remember her telling me with moist eyes, “Herz, must we separate? We lived together; can't we die together?” I had no answer for that.

Herz sat beside his wife. It was after a long time he was next to her. She looked so different when she left the coasts of war- struck Amsterdam. Renata had wrinkled pale skin. She sat dreadfully still and stared into the infinity. Her lifeless face showed no emotion. He tried to talk with her. What followed was a monologue- “Dear Renata, I know you are upset with me. You have every reason to. I am sorry. I gave up. I should have kept searching for you,” he paused to take a deep breath as his voice choked. That evening, the nurse entered the room again and administered Renata with medicines. She looked at Herz. His eyes revealed that he was desperately searching for answers. He deserved to know. “I have been in the service of your wife for 10 years now. I didn’t doubt that you were her husband for a second. Despite not remembering big portions of her past, your wife accurately remembers that she had a loved one for whom she is waiting. Once every one or two months, she would, all of a sudden, start writing a letter. It was the same content, addressed to an unknown, and signed as waiting. Every letter looked identical to the previous. Over the course of 10 years, she wrote 75 letters. Since they were addressed to an unknown, we didn't know what to do with them. I still kept them for the record."

As soon as I set foot on the soil of the New World, I knew it was not going to be easy. A visit to the Refugee Shelter changed my doubts into realities. A homeless Jew in foreign soil, who had just had a very narrow escape from the Holocaust. What possibly could I do? I checked all records of every refugee that landed in America in the last five years. I visited every refugee shelter on the East coast. I had some relatives in Georgia. I tried contacting them, but in vain. The mystery was killing me slowly. It was then that one day a successful newspaper published the names of all refugees who had died during travel to or by disease in the States. One of them talked of a middle-aged lady whose name was Rita. A part of me died that day. It was not impossible that they were talking of Renata and had misprinted the name. Unfortunately, they had no information more than what they had published. It took me three years to finally accept the fact you were gone, my love: snatched away from me by the War.

Two months later, Renata was sitting on an arm chair in the veranda of the Nursing Home. She was reading the newspaper. Renata's health was improving steadily. She looked closer to her age now. As she sat and handled her newspaper to season the streak of sunlight pouring in, she squinted her eyes to read better. Despite being able to read again, and with her health improving, memory had not arrived yet. She would forget everything, where the door to the room was, what she was asked a minute ago, even what her name was. December 5, 1971 IN THE INDO- PAKISTAN WAR OF 1971, USA TAKES A STAND! As soon as she read the news, her hands began shivering. The newspaper crackled as she shook it violently. Grief flashed on her face. Renata was in a flood of tears. Reading the word ‘War’ affected her significantly. "Renata! What's wrong my dear? You are safe here, we are all safe here, and together. I will never leave you again. Please recognize me, I am your love, Herz, your Herz . . ."

I think about her all the time. I am still staying in Oswego, New York and visit the Emergency Refugee shelter every week with the hope that my Renata would be there some day. I will never forgive myself for doing that to Renata. I should never have left her alone. It was not the War, it was I who shattered our small lives!

14 February, 1972. A date Herz would never forget. As a part of his weekly practice, Herz was holding Renata’s hand and taking her for a walk among the Sugar Maple, Red Cedar and Green Ash in the deciduous parks. Being in the serenity of parks helped Renata a lot. After the 75 minute walk, they would return to the Nursing Home. On the table in her room, was kept a very dusty old letter. Renata picked up the letter and felt it with her hands, drawing it closer to her face, she closed her eyes and took a deep breath to draw in every scent of the old paper. The letter had just been delivered, but surprisingly felt familiar. Had she crossed paths with it before? She opened her eyes and read the letter. The letter was very old and was tinge of pale yellow. It was torn and at some places even burnt on the sides. Regardless of all the harm. The hand script still was neat and filled with beauty. It took no notice of how uneven and ugly the edges of the letter had become. As soon she finished reading the letter, she lifted her head and looked at Herz. She stretched her hand to give the letter to its recipient. In the golden hour, her eyes glistened with tears. "You have come, Herz! You have returned, you have fulfilled your promise! "

Dear love, It would give you immense pleasure to know that I have reached the United States of America safely. For four months, I lived in the Refugee’s Shelter. Later, I decided to move to Philadelphia. I have also received a proposal for job. Come to America as soon as possible, Herz. A new, fresh start awaits us here. The address for our home in Philadelphia would be: 621 Halleon Way 25 Drive St., Philadelphia. Waiting for you to fulfil your promise. Love, Renata. Date: 12th of August, 1944. Name & address: Herz Berger, Prinsengracht 1024 GV Amsterdam Netherlands.
The letter took 27 years to reach the right hands.

items.text_en: The telephone kept on the table beside the bed rang sharply.
The black polished telephone contrasted the brilliantly lit white room.
The nurse came in from the other room and answered.
“Hullo? Renata?” “May I know who I am speaking to please?” “May I speak to Renata Berger please?
I am her husband, Herz Berger.
Tell her my name, she would recognize.” The burgundy colored train with the yellow characters ‘PENNSYLVANIA’ stopped on the station of Philadelphia.
Herz Berger stepped out of the passenger coach of second class.
He had a long black overcoat draped over his hunched back.
There was a silhouette of a six-point star etched on his coat.
At one time, there was The Star of David sown there.
It was just the shadow left now.
A long white beard overlapped the overcoat.
Mr. Berger walked slowly, measuring every step judiciously.
The telephone kept on the table beside the bed rang sharply.
The black polished telephone contrasted the brilliantly lit white room.
The nurse came in from the other room and answered.
“Hullo? Renata?” “May I know who I am speaking to please?” “May I speak to Renata Berger please?
I am her husband, Herz Berger.
Tell her my name, she would recognize.” The burgundy colored train with the yellow characters ‘PENNSYLVANIA’ stopped on the station of Philadelphia.
Herz Berger stepped out of the passenger coach of second class.
He had a long black overcoat draped over his hunched back.
There was a silhouette of a six-point star etched on his coat.
At one time, there was The Star of David sown there.
It was just the shadow left now.
A long white beard overlapped the overcoat.
Mr Berger walked slowly, measuring every step judiciously.
Herz was brought into the small room by the nurse.
Renata sat on the bed, facing on the other side, staring at the wall.
She was in a long black frock with grey hair tied in an untidy bun.
“Renata?” He whispered from underneath the unkempt mustache.
“Mr. Berger, I told you that Mrs.
Berger is suffering from Retrograde amnesia.
She does not even remember her name.
That is exactly why she has been kept in this nursing home.” Herz tilted his head towards the nurse, still looking at the ground.
Tears welled up in his wrinkled eyes.
It took him great courage to ask, “Is there any chance she can get better?”
“Renata, I promise I will see you very soon,” I said at the Port of Amsterdam as she prepared to leave with some fellow Jews.
I knew sending her to the New World was not safe, especially with German U- boats scanning the Atlantic.
But I had no other alternative to ensure she survives.
She would wait for me there.
She would live in the Emergency Refugee Shelter in New York.
As soon as the war is over, I would travel there too.
I remember her telling me with moist eyes, “Herz, must we separate?
We lived together; can't we die together?” I had no answer for that.
Herz sat beside his wife.
It was after a long time he was next to her.
She looked so different when she left the coasts of war- struck Amsterdam.
Renata had wrinkled pale skin.
She sat dreadfully still and stared into the infinity.
Her lifeless face showed no emotion.
He tried to talk with her.
What followed was a monologue- “Dear Renata, I know you are upset with me.
You have every reason to.
I am sorry.
I gave up.
I should have kept searching for you,” he paused to take a deep breath as his voice choked.
That evening, the nurse entered the room again and administered Renata with medicines.
She looked at Herz.
His eyes revealed that he was desperately searching for answers.
He deserved to know.
“I have been in the service of your wife for 10 years now.
I didn’t doubt that you were her husband for a second.
Despite not remembering big portions of her past, your wife accurately remembers that she had a loved one for whom she is waiting.
Once every one or two months, she would, all of a sudden, start writing a letter.
It was the same content, addressed to an unknown, and signed as waiting.
Every letter looked identical to the previous.
Over the course of 10 years, she wrote 75 letters.
Since they were addressed to an unknown, we didn't know what to do with them.
I still kept them for the record."
As soon as I set foot on the soil of the New World, I knew it was not going to be easy.
A visit to the Refugee Shelter changed my doubts into realities.
A homeless Jew in foreign soil, who had just had a very narrow escape from the Holocaust.
What possibly could I do?
I checked all records of every refugee that landed in America in the last five years.
I visited every refugee shelter on the East coast.
I had some relatives in Georgia.
I tried contacting them, but in vain.
The mystery was killing me slowly.
It was then that one day a successful newspaper published the names of all refugees who had died during travel to or by disease in the States.
One of them talked of a middle-aged lady whose name was Rita.
A part of me died that day.
It was not impossible that they were talking of Renata and had misprinted the name.
Unfortunately, they had no information more than what they had published.
It took me three years to finally accept the fact you were gone, my love: snatched away from me by the War.
Two months later, Renata was sitting on an arm chair in the veranda of the Nursing Home.
She was reading the newspaper.
Renata's health was improving steadily.
She looked closer to her age now.
As she sat and handled her newspaper to season the streak of sunlight pouring in, she squinted her eyes to read better.
Despite being able to read again, and with her health improving, memory had not arrived yet.
She would forget everything, where the door to the room was, what she was asked a minute ago, even what her name was.
December 5, 1971 IN THE INDO- PAKISTAN WAR OF 1971, USA TAKES A STAND!
As soon as she read the news, her hands began shivering.
The newspaper crackled as she shook it violently.
Grief flashed on her face.
Renata was in a flood of tears.
Reading the word ‘War’ affected her significantly.
"Renata! What's wrong my dear?
You are safe here, we are all safe here, and together.
I will never leave you again.
Please recognize me, I am your love, Herz, your Herz . . ."
I think about her all the time.
I am still staying in Oswego, New York and visit the Emergency Refugee shelter every week with the hope that my Renata would be there some day.
I will never forgive myself for doing that to Renata.
I should never have left her alone.
It was not the War, it was I who shattered our small lives!
14 February, 1972.
A date Herz would never forget.
As a part of his weekly practice, Herz was holding Renata’s hand and taking her for a walk among the Sugar Maple, Red Cedar and Green Ash in the deciduous parks.
Being in the serenity of parks helped Renata a lot.
After the 75 minute walk, they would return to the Nursing Home.
On the table in her room, was kept a very dusty old letter.
Renata picked up the letter and felt it with her hands, drawing it closer to her face, she closed her eyes and took a deep breath to draw in every scent of the old paper.
The letter had just been delivered, but surprisingly felt familiar.
Had she crossed paths with it before?
She opened her eyes and read the letter.
The letter was very old and was tinge of pale yellow.
It was torn and at some places even burnt on the sides.
Regardless of all the harm.
The hand script still was neat and filled with beauty.
It took no notice of how uneven and ugly the edges of the letter had become.
As soon she finished reading the letter, she lifted her head and looked at Herz.
She stretched her hand to give the letter to its recipient.
In the golden hour, her eyes glistened with tears.
"You have come, Herz!
You have returned, you have fulfilled your promise! "
Dear love, It would give you immense pleasure to know that I have reached the United States of America safely.
For four months, I lived in the Refugee’s Shelter.
Later, I decided to move to Philadelphia.
I have also received a proposal for job.
Come to America as soon as possible, Herz.
A new, fresh start awaits us here.
The address for our home in Philadelphia would be: 621 Halleon Way 25 Drive St., Philadelphia.
Waiting for you to fulfil your promise.
Love, Renata. Date: 12th of August, 1944.
Name & address: Herz Berger, Prinsengracht 1024 GV Amsterdam Netherlands.
The letter took 27 years to reach the right hands.
